title: Orthonormal Basis
body:
An **orthogonal set** is a set of non-zero vectors that are pairwise orthogonal. Make them all
unit length and it is **orthonormal**:

$$
\mathbf{u}_i \cdot \mathbf{u}_j = \begin{cases} 1 & i = j \\ 0 & i \neq j \end{cases}
$$

An orthogonal set is automatically [[Linear Dependence|independent]], so any $n$ of them in
$\mathbb{R}^n$ are a [[Basis]] with no checking required. [[Basis]] (MATH 1203) states the
coordinate formula; this note is about why orthonormality is worth paying for and what an
orthogonal *matrix* does.

## Why it is worth paying for

Coordinates in a general basis mean solving $B\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{v}$, an $O(n^3)$
[[Gaussian Elimination]]. In an orthonormal basis they are dot products:

$$
c_i = \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i
$$

$O(n)$ each, independent of one another, and **truncatable**: keep the first $k$ coefficients and
you have the best $k$-dimensional approximation, because dropping a term only drops its own
contribution. In a skewed basis the coefficients interact and truncating is meaningless. That
single property is what makes [[Low-Rank Approximation]], [[Principal Component Analysis]],
[[Fourier Series]], and JPEG compression all possible.

Numerically it matters just as much. Orthonormal bases preserve lengths and angles, so they
neither amplify nor destroy rounding error, which is why serious numerical software factors into
orthogonal pieces ([[Gram-Schmidt|QR]], [[Singular Value Decomposition|SVD]]) rather than
inverting.

## Orthogonal matrices

Put an orthonormal basis in the columns of a square $Q$. Then $Q^TQ = I$, so

$$
Q^{-1} = Q^T
$$

**The inverse is the transpose.** No [[Matrix Inverse|inversion]] to compute, ever. Such a $Q$ is
an **orthogonal matrix**, and the name is a historical annoyance: the columns are orthonormal,
not merely orthogonal.

Geometrically $Q$ is a **rigid motion**: $\|Q\mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{x}\|$ and $Q\mathbf{x}\cdot
Q\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}$, so lengths and angles survive. That leaves only
rotations and reflections, separated by $\det Q = \pm 1$. This is the fact
[[Singular Value Decomposition]] leans on when it reads $A = U\Sigma V^T$ as rotate, stretch,
rotate.

For a non-square $Q$ ($n \times k$, $k < n$) you get $Q^TQ = I_k$ but $QQ^T \neq I_n$; $QQ^T$ is
the [[Projection]] onto the column space instead. Worth keeping straight, since truncated
factorisations are always the non-square case.

## Getting one

- [[Gram-Schmidt]]: turn any basis into an orthonormal one by subtracting off projections.
- [[Spectral Theorem]]: a symmetric matrix hands you one made of its own eigenvectors.
- [[Singular Value Decomposition]]: hands you two, one for the input space and one for the output.

## Related

- [[Basis]] and [[Dot Product]] (MATH 1203)
- [[Projection]]: the formula that only works here
- [[Orthogonal Functions]] (MATH 4199): the same idea with an integral inner product, where
  $\{1, \cos nx, \sin nx\}$ is the orthonormal basis and [[Fourier Coefficients]] are the
  coordinates
- [[Inner Product]]: orthonormality is stated with $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, so it transfers
